title: Latency Sleuth: Hybrid Trace Harvester
content:
Purpose and context:

This is an ad-hoc runbook + working notes for a hybrid trace collector we use when a production latency spike or tail-regression appears and the regular CI perf jobs don't surface an obvious hotspot. The goal is to capture correlated user-request traces, kernel-level samples, and lightweight eBPF events with a single coordinated invocation so we can stitch: wall-clock request flow, CPU stacks, syscalls, and scheduler delays.

When to use:
- Intermittent 95/99p tail latency increases only reproducible on production traffic patterns or long-batched workloads.
- When deployment rollouts correlate with latency shape changes but microbenchmarks look fine.
- Before starting a disruptive rollback, capture full-context artifacts.

High-level approach:
1) Light request-tagging at ingress (temporary header X-Latency-Sleuth: <run-id>) to correlate logs/traces and to filter sampling in downstream services.
2) Short-lived request-level sampling (1 in N) using router/ingress rate limiter hooks — keep sampling fraction low to reduce cost and noise.
3) On sampled requests, trigger a collector pod (or sidecar) that:
   a) launches perf (or async-profiler) for user-space stacks, configured for CPU and async-java if applicable;
   b) attaches a BPFTrace/eBPF probe for sched/sleep/syscall latencies and queue lengths;
   c) emits a compact pprof (cpu/alloc) and raw perf.data;
   d) records a small kernel trace (ftrace) for IO and context switches (capped to 10s).
4) Push artifacts to S3 with a consistent prefix: /perf-sleuth/<run-id>/<hostname>/<pid>/

Collector orchestration (script sketch) - keep idempotent and limited to 15s capture window:
- env RUN_ID=$(uuidgen)
- curl -X POST http://router.local/sampling-hook -d "run_id=$RUN_ID&headers=X-Latency-Sleuth"
- spawn collector with: --duration=12 --perf-interval=1ms --ebpf-filter="comm == \"runtime\" || pid==${TARGET_PID}"

Perf and flamegraph notes:
- Use perf record -F 400 -p PID -g -- sleep 12 to capture callgraphs; prefer -F 400 on busy hosts and reduce to 100 on quiet ones.
- For Java/Managed runtimes prefer async-profiler (keeps wall-clock stacks and resolves JIT frames).
- Convert perf.data to folded stacks for flamegraph: perf script | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded; then flamegraph.pl out.folded > flame.svg.
- Ensure kernel symbols available (debuginfo) or use addr2line for triage.

eBPF probes to collect (recommended small set):
- sched:sched_switch (capture latency between runnable -> running)
- tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_open and sys_exit_open (for suspicious FS waits)
- tcp:tcp_probe (if networking suspected) with caps on number of events (--max-events 10000)
- tracepoint:block:block_rq_issue and block_rq_complete (to see IO queues)

BPFTrace example snippet (save as sleuth.bt) - keep it conservative:
- BEGIN { printf("SLEUTH %s start\n", ENV->RUN_ID); }
- tracepoint:sched:sched_switch /comm == "runtime"/ { @[comm] = count(); }
- tracepoint:block:block_rq_issue { @[disk] = hist(blk_rq_sectors); }
- END { print(@); }

Artifact naming and metadata (important for triage):
- filename convention: <run-id>__<service>__<host>__<timestamp>__<type>.tar.gz
- include metadata.json inside tar with: run_id, sample_rate, trigger_headers, git_sha, kernel_version, container_runtime, cpu_freq_governor

Storage and retention guidance:
- Keep raw perf/perf.data and eBPF event logs for 7 days by default, pprof + flamegraphs for 30 days.
- Upload compressed tar.gz to perf-sleuth bucket with lifecycle policy: raw->30d cold->90d delete unless ticket attached.

CI integration and perf job recipe (for later automation):
- Make a perf-job template that can be invoked with: job_type=ad-hoc-sleuth, sample_fraction=0.01, duration=12s, probes=[sched,block].
- The job should produce: flame.svg, pprof.pb.gz, perf.data.gz, ebpf.log, metadata.json and a short summary note (top 5 hot symbols, top syscalls, top block devices).

Triage checklist (quick runbook):
1) Confirm run_id and retrieve tar from bucket.
2) Look at metadata.json for sample_rate and target pid/service.
3) Open flame.svg and inspect wide, high stacks at top; note function names and inlining.
4) Correlate with logs: grep for X-Latency-Sleuth: <run-id> to find request IDs and timings.
5) Inspect eBPF summaries for syscalls and block latencies; look for 100us+ hist buckets.
6) If perf stacks are kernel-heavy, check for scheduling or IRQ storms (dmesg, iowait).

Common pitfalls and mitigations:
- Too high sampling rate: noisy artifacts and overhead. Start 0.1% and raise if signal weak.
- Large perf captures on multi-core machines can be huge. Use -F limit and narrow -p PID + --call-graph dwarf to reduce size.
- eBPF scripts with open histograms can blow memory — always specify aggregates limits and max-events.
- JIT symbol resolution fails: ensure java/native debug symbols or use async-profiler agent to resolve names at runtime.

Follow-ups and improvements backlog:
- Add small agent that can atomically toggle perf collection on a pod given run_id via sidecar API (avoid SSH).
- Automate symbol upload so flamegraphs resolve in the web UI.
- Provide a lightweight web UI for browsing sleuth artifacts (search by run_id, tag by ticket).

Notes and references:
- Async-profiler guide: https://github.com/jvm-profiling-tools/async-profiler
- Brendan Gregg flamegraphs: http://www.brendangregg.com/flamegraphs.html
- BPFTrace cookbook snippets (internal): confluence link above

Quick command reference (copyable):
- perf capture: perf record -F 400 -p $PID -g -- sleep 12 && perf archive -o perf-$RUN_ID.tar.gz
- convert: perf script | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded && ./flamegraph.pl out.folded > flame-$RUN_ID.svg
- bpftrace: sudo bpftrace sleuth.bt -c "sleep 12" > ebpf-$RUN_ID.log

If you run this and the artifact points to a kernel or scheduler issue, please ping eng-sre and attach the run_id + one-line summary in the ticket.

Author: Maya Chen (serving-runtime perf lead)
